projects.title: Online Travel Agency (OTA) Platform
projects.description: Web-based travel booking platform enabling users to search, compare, and book flights from multiple airlines and GDS systems
projects.longDescription: A comprehensive travel booking platform integrating multiple airlines (Novo Air, US-Bangla Airlines, Jazeera Airways, AirAstra, Air Arabia, IndiGo) and Global Distribution Systems (Amadeus, Sabre, Travelport). Built with scalable microservices architecture to handle high-volume flight searches and bookings.
projects.body:
## What it does

A multi-tenant OTA platform that lets travel agencies search, compare, book, and manage flights, hotels, holiday packages, and other travel services. One codebase serves multiple client brands with isolated configuration, supporting both B2B and B2C business models.

## Scale

- **6 live client brands** — TripLover, TravelChamp, FirstTrip, TakeTrip, TakeOff, and TripLover Dubai
- **36+ services** in the ecosystem, built for high availability and fault tolerance
- **30 integrated GDS/NDC suppliers** — a single flight search fans out to all of them and returns 200-300 feeds spanning 40-50 unique airlines
- Airline and GDS coverage including Amadeus, Sabre, Travelport, Novo Air, US-Bangla Airlines, Jazeera Airways, AirAstra, Air Arabia, and IndiGo

## My role

I architected and led development of the multi-tenant SaaS platform. Beyond the core architecture, I:

- Led the migration of the core database from SQL Server to PostgreSQL, cutting licensing costs and unblocking Linux hosting
- Migrated 8 legacy .NET Framework applications to .NET Core for cross-platform deployment
- Built an automated xUnit API integration test suite covering 30+ supplier integration projects
- Integrated APM monitoring with Elasticsearch-based structured logging, **cutting production failure rates by 30%**
- Implemented Progressive Search, Search Ranking, Universal Split PNR, Refund Reissue, and PNR Details
- Contributed to CI/CD pipelines and code reviews, and mentored new team members

## Why this stack

A **modular monolith** on .NET Core rather than full microservices — the modules share a deployment boundary while staying independently maintainable, which suits a platform where a single search has to coordinate 30 suppliers with low latency. **Dapper** over EF Core keeps the hot search path close to raw SQL. **RabbitMQ** decouples the long-running booking and ticketing workflows, with MSSQL and MongoDB each serving the workloads they fit.

## Proof of work documents

projects.title: Foodi CRM - Food Delivery System
projects.description: Full-stack customer relationship management system for food delivery businesses
projects.longDescription: Foodi CRM is a comprehensive customer relationship management system for food delivery businesses, enabling order tracking, restaurant management, delivery partner monitoring, and customer interaction. Built with a scalable microservices architecture focused on performance and usability.
projects.body:
## What it does

A food delivery platform and the CRM behind it — customers browse restaurants, place orders, pay, and track deliveries in real time, while the operations team manages restaurants, delivery partners, and customer communication from one place.

## My role

I designed and developed the **Engagement Automation** feature for Foodi-CRM, streamlining the communication workflows between customers and the operations team. I also implemented a **read/write Redis caching strategy** that improved API response times and made the platform more scalable under load.

## Why this stack

A genuine microservices split here, unlike the OTA platform's modular monolith — ordering, delivery tracking, and CRM have different scaling profiles and change at different rates. **Kafka and RabbitMQ** carry the event flow between them: order placed, driver assigned, status changed. Polyglot by design — .NET Core and EF Core for the transactional core, **Go** and **Node.js** where throughput or ecosystem fit mattered more, PostgreSQL underneath, React on the front.

projects.title: Recruiter.Bdjobs.com
projects.description: Hiring management platform allowing employers to manage job posting to online assessments and interviews
projects.longDescription: A comprehensive recruitment platform that allows employers to manage the entire hiring process from job posting to online assessments and interviews. Built with Angular frontend and ASP.NET Core backend, integrated with Bangladesh's largest job portal ecosystem.
projects.body:
## What it does

The employer side of Bdjobs.com, Bangladesh's largest job portal — a hiring platform covering the full recruitment workflow from posting a job through online assessments and interviews, with application management and resume handling in between.

## My role

I worked with product, backend, and QA teams to migrate the Bdjobs.com corporate panel from **legacy ASP to Angular and ASP.NET Core**, modernizing the stack while keeping a high-traffic platform running.

I built two features that moved the business number directly — the **Employer Job Posting and Hiring System** and the **Candidate SkillMatch Score** — which together **increased platform sales by 17%**.

I also implemented a **CQRS-style architecture with an ETL pipeline** that separated the read and write databases for job listings, and optimized queries to cut search time.

## Why this stack

Angular and ASP.NET Core were the target of the legacy-ASP migration, so the choice was set by where the platform was heading. The interesting decision was architectural rather than technological: employers posting jobs and job seekers searching them are two workloads with opposite needs, and forcing both through one normalized MSSQL schema was what made search slow. The ETL split let each side have the shape it wanted.

projects.title: Airline Supplier Integration Projects
projects.description: 8 cloud-native supplier integration projects connecting OTA platforms with major airlines and GDS systems
projects.longDescription: Developed 8 cloud-native supplier integration projects (Sabre, Travelport, Travelport NDC, Air India, Flydubai, SQ NDC, TK NDC, Indigo) to integrate supplier APIs into client OTA platforms. These integrations increased flight search feed by 27% and enabled seamless booking across multiple airline systems.
projects.body:
## What it does

Eight cloud-native integration projects that connect OTA platforms to airline and GDS supplier APIs: **Sabre, Travelport, Travelport NDC, Air India, Flydubai, SQ NDC, TK NDC, and IndiGo**.

## Scale

These integrations **increased the flight search feed by 27%** — more suppliers answering a search means more inventory and better fares reaching the user.

## My role

Delivered all eight. Each supplier exposes its own protocol, authentication model, and data shape, so each integration is a separate normalization problem behind a common internal contract — which is what lets the search pipeline treat 30 suppliers as one feed.

I also built the automated xUnit API integration test suite that covers these projects, so supplier behaviour changes surface at release validation rather than in production.

## Why this stack

Deliberately split into separate cloud-native services rather than folded into the platform: suppliers change their APIs on their own schedules, and a failure or redeploy for one must not touch the other 29. The mix of **REST, SOAP, and NDC** isn't a choice so much as the reality of what each supplier offers.

projects.title: Fare Comparison
projects.description: Airline fare intelligence platform comparing competitors' real-time fares, flight schedules, and seat availability for data-driven pricing
projects.longDescription: An airline fare intelligence platform that enables airlines to compare competitors' real time fares, flight schedules, and seat availability, providing data-driven pricing recommendations to maximize revenue and profitability. Integrated multiple GDS and NDC suppliers to aggregate and normalize competitor data, and engineered pricing-intelligence logic to help airlines optimize ticket pricing.
projects.body:
## What it does

An airline fare intelligence platform. Airlines use it to see what competitors are charging in real time — fares, flight schedules, and seat availability — and get data-driven pricing recommendations from that picture.

## My role

I designed and built the platform end to end, from the supplier integrations through to the React dashboard airlines actually work in.

The integration layer pulls from **multiple GDS and NDC suppliers**, each returning data in its own shape and updating constantly. A large part of the work was normalizing those feeds into something comparable. On top of that I engineered the **pricing-intelligence logic** that analyzes the aggregated market data and generates fare recommendations.

## Why this stack

**Hangfire** drives the recurring collection jobs — competitor fares have to be pulled continuously, not on demand, so the dashboard reads from data that is already there. **EF Core** rather than Dapper here, because this is a write-heavy aggregation workload where schema modelling matters more than raw read latency. PostgreSQL stores the normalized fare history that the comparison logic runs against.

projects.title: O2P — A Reliable Oracle-to-PostgreSQL Data Migration Tool
projects.description: I built O2P to solve one of the highest-risk parts of a large Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration: moving large, changing production datasets reliably without turning every table into a manual migration exercise.
projects.body:
| Role | Designed and built the O2P migration tool |
| --- | --- |
| Problem | Reliable, observable and recoverable Oracle → PostgreSQL data migration |
| Stack | .NET 8 · React · Oracle · PostgreSQL · Oracle LogMiner |
| Migration Context | ~1 TB · 550+ tables · 1,700+ database objects · 23 applications |
| Key Capabilities | Parallel batch copy · retry/recovery · validation · progress tracking · incremental catch-up |
| Outcome | Turned data migration into a controlled, repeatable workflow instead of one-off transfers |

At production scale, that becomes a different engineering problem.

Some tables are huge. Some contain LOBs. A transfer can fail after running for hours. Running too many copies in parallel can overload the Oracle source. Meanwhile, the source may continue changing while the baseline migration is running.

A simple script could move rows, but it could not answer the operational questions that mattered:

What has already completed?
Where exactly did a failed migration stop?
Can I retry without loading committed data twice?
How much parallelism is safe for the source database?
How do I know the destination is complete?
What happens to changes made after the initial copy starts?
I built O2P (Oracle to PostgreSQL) to make those concerns part of the migration system itself.

What O2P Does
O2P discovers Oracle tables, prepares PostgreSQL targets, divides large tables into manageable batches, copies them with controlled parallelism, tracks execution state, validates results, and can catch up later source changes for eligible tables.

sections.body:
The goal was not simply **maximum transfer speed**. The goal was **controlled throughput with recoverability and visibility**.

## How It Works

### 1. Discover and prepare

O2P reads Oracle metadata, discovers tables and columns, and maps supported Oracle types to PostgreSQL types. An operator can migrate a full schema or select individual tables.

### 2. Break large tables into batches

Instead of treating a large table as one long operation, O2P plans smaller units of work. Depending on the table, it can use ROWID ranges, partitions, numeric primary-key ranges, or fallback strategies.

This reduces the failure boundary: one failed batch does not automatically mean starting an entire large table again.

### 3. Copy with bounded parallelism

Workers stream Oracle rows into PostgreSQL using binary COPY. Concurrency, Oracle sessions, batch sizes and optional throughput limits are bounded.

This was an important design decision: **migration speed should not come at the cost of destabilizing the production source**.

### 4. Make retries safer

Execution state is persisted instead of living only in process memory. Each committed PostgreSQL batch also receives a target-side marker.

If the process is interrupted, O2P can determine which work is still pending and avoid blindly loading an already committed batch again.

### 5. Validate the result

After bulk migration, O2P compares source and destination row counts and stores the validation result.

Row counts are intentionally treated as a **migration gate, not absolute proof of data correctness**. Critical migrations still require business-level and application-level validation.

### 6. Catch up later changes

For eligible tables, O2P can use Oracle LogMiner to identify changes after the baseline copy and apply the current row state to PostgreSQL.

This is an **on-demand catch-up mechanism**, not a continuous replication platform. Oracle LogMiner analyzes redo information and has logging/configuration prerequisites.

## Engineering Decisions That Mattered

**Batches instead of whole-table jobs.** Smaller batches create smaller failure domains, measurable progress and more practical retries.

**Bounded concurrency instead of maximum concurrency.** More workers can improve throughput, but they also increase source sessions and database pressure. O2P treats concurrency as a controlled resource.

**Streaming instead of loading tables into memory.** A bounded producer/consumer pipeline keeps memory usage predictable while Oracle reads and PostgreSQL writes proceed concurrently.

**Target-side commit markers.** A Worker can fail immediately after PostgreSQL commits. Recording a batch marker in the target transaction provides stronger evidence of completion than relying only on Worker state.

**Bulk copy plus explicit catch-up.** O2P separates the baseline copy from an explicit change-capture step instead of pretending a long-running migration is automatically one consistent snapshot.

## Impact

The most important impact was operational: **data movement became a repeatable process that could be observed, controlled and recovered**, rather than a sequence of manually managed transfers.

O2P introduced visible table- and batch-level progress, controlled Oracle source pressure, smaller failure boundaries, persistent retry state, protection against reloading committed batches, source/target row-count validation, and an incremental catch-up path for eligible tables.

O2P was built as part of a broader production migration covering approximately **1 TB of data, 550+ tables, 1,700+ database objects and 23 applications** within **13 working days**.

The wider migration reported **no migration-related bugs in QA or after deployment**. That outcome reflects the entire migration effort—including database conversion, application changes, testing and validation—not O2P alone.

## Run O2P Yourself

Clone the [O2P GitHub repository](https://github.com/developerhridu/O2P) and use this quick start for a local test migration. You need the .NET 8 SDK, Node.js/npm, Docker, access to an Oracle source, and a PostgreSQL 14+ target. Create the target schema before starting.

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/developerhridu/O2P.git
cd O2P
$env:O2P_METADATA_PASSWORD = "<strong-metadata-password>"
docker compose up -d metadata-pg
```

Open three terminals in the cloned project directory. Use **the same metadata password** in the first two.

**Terminal 1 — API**

```powershell
$env:ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT = "Development"
$env:ConnectionStrings__MetadataDb = "Host=127.0.0.1;Port=7936;Database=nonoraclemigrationdb;Username=nonoraclemigrationdb;Password=<strong-metadata-password>"
$env:JwtSettings__Secret = "<at-least-32-random-characters>"
$env:BootstrapAdmin__Password = "<strong-admin-password>"
dotnet run --project src/O2P.Api --launch-profile http
```

**Terminal 2 — Worker**

```powershell
$env:DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT = "Development"
$env:ConnectionStrings__MetadataDb = "Host=127.0.0.1;Port=7936;Database=nonoraclemigrationdb;Username=nonoraclemigrationdb;Password=<strong-metadata-password>"
dotnet run --project src/O2P.Worker
```

**Terminal 3 — web UI**

```powershell
cd web
npm ci
npm run dev
```

Open **http://localhost:5151** after the API reports that metadata setup is complete. Sign in as `admin` with the admin password you set above, then change it when prompted.

To migrate data:

1. In **Connections**, add and test an Oracle source and PostgreSQL target.
2. In **Migrations**, create a migration and bind those connections to the source and target slots.
3. Discover the Oracle schema, select the tables, and review the mapped columns and target schema.
4. Start a run against a **test target**. Watch progress in **Runs**, then check every table's row-count result and independently inspect important data.

O2P moves selected table schemas and rows. Oracle procedures, views, triggers, sequences, and application code require separate migration work.


---

**Technologies:** Oracle · PostgreSQL 14+ · .NET 8 · React · Oracle LogMiner · PostgreSQL Binary COPY · EF Core · ASP.NET Data Protection

projects.title: Booking Manager Service
projects.description: Background service that automatically cancels un-ticketed bookings, saving ~$23K-$27K total across 6 OTA clients
projects.longDescription: Developed a critical background service using ASP.NET Core & Hangfire that automatically cancels un-ticketed bookings before the last ticketing time. This solution reduced ADM penalties by $4,500-$6,400 per month per OTA, achieving total savings of ~$23,000-$27,000 across 6 clients.
projects.body:
## What it does

A background service that watches bookings approaching their last ticketing time and automatically cancels the ones still un-ticketed — before the airline can charge an Agency Debit Memo penalty for holding them.

## Scale

Running across **6 OTA client platforms**, it reduced ADM penalties by **$4,500-$6,400 per month per OTA**, for a total saving of roughly **$23,000-$27,000**.

## My role

Built it end to end.

## Why this stack

**Hangfire** on ASP.NET Core for recurring job scheduling with retry semantics, backed by **SQLite** for persistence — deliberately lightweight, since the service only needs to survive restarts with its own job state intact, not share a database with the platform it protects. Keeping it isolated means a problem here can't take the booking flow down with it.

## Proof of work documents
